clinicalPearls: Characterised by ophthalmoplegia from involvement of the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves together with visual loss from optic nerve involvement
The distinguishing feature from superior orbital fissure syndrome is the addition of optic neuropathy, since the optic canal lies at the apex
Sensory loss follows the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and proptosis may be present with an orbital mass
A relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced acuity or colour vision reflect the optic nerve component
Common causes include invasive infection such as mucormycosis and aspergillosis, tumour, and inflammatory disease
Aggressive fungal orbital apex infection must be considered urgently in diabetic or immunocompromised patients
Imaging of the orbit and skull base is essential to define the responsible lesion
reference.pathophysiology: The orbital apex is the crowded posterior region of the orbit where the superior orbital fissure and the optic canal converge, transmitting the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery alongside the ocular motor nerves, the ophthalmic trigeminal branches, and sympathetic fibres. A lesion here compresses or infiltrates these structures, combining an ophthalmoplegia and trigeminal sensory disturbance with an optic neuropathy that causes visual loss. Responsible processes include invasive fungal and bacterial infection, neoplasm, granulomatous and other inflammatory disease, trauma, and vascular lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Superior orbital fissure syndrome without optic nerve involvement
Thyroid eye disease with apical crowding
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the orbit and skull base with contrast
CT of the orbit and paranasal sinuses to assess bone and sinus disease
Nasoendoscopy and biopsy where invasive fungal infection is suspected
Blood glucose and immune status assessment
Visual field testing and assessment of the afferent pupillary pathway
redFlags: Rapidly progressive signs in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient suggesting invasive fungal infection needing emergency management
Acute visual loss requiring urgent evaluation of the optic nerve
Signs of orbital cellulitis or abscess
Features of malignant infiltration of the skull base
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the cause and speed of treatment; invasive infection carries high morbidity and mortality without prompt intervention, whereas inflammatory causes may respond to treatment, though optic nerve damage can leave permanent visual loss.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise optic nerve involvement that distinguishes it from superior orbital fissure syndrome
Delaying diagnosis of invasive fungal infection in an at-risk patient
Attributing the picture to inflammation and giving steroids before excluding infection and tumour
Underestimating the urgency of associated visual loss
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause, guided by urgent contrast imaging and biopsy

For invasive fungal infection (mucormycosis, aspergillosis) give emergency systemic antifungal therapy (liposomal amphotericin B) with surgical debridement and correction of diabetes, ketoacidosis and immunosuppression
Treat bacterial infection with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and drainage of any collection

Treat inflammatory or granulomatous causes (idiopathic orbital inflammation, IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis) with systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression as needed
Manage neoplastic causes with tissue diagnosis followed by surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy as appropriate
Monitor visual acuity, colour vision and the afferent pupillary pathway for optic-nerve compromise
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across ophthalmology, ENT, neurology and oncology with urgent escalation for aggressive infection
